opus-5.5.text:
I think it's one of the most underappreciated problems in the field right now. Everyone's excited about the models (the architectures, the scaling, the parameter counts), but in biology the model is really only as good as the experimental lens you used to generate the data.

Here's the core issue: most biological data we have was collected to answer a specific question, in a specific cell type, under specific conditions, with a specific assay. So when you train a model on it, you're inheriting all of those choices as hidden assumptions. If your perturbation data comes mostly from immortalized cancer cell lines like K562 or HEK293, your model is going to learn the biology of those cells really well, and it may not generalize to a primary T cell or a neuron or a hepatocyte in a living tissue. The model doesn't know what it doesn't know.

Then there's the readout problem. If you only measure RNA, you're blind to a lot of what's happening at the protein level, post-translational modifications, localization, cell-cell interactions, timing. Transcriptomics is wonderful because it's scalable and cheap per measurement, which is why so much of the field has converged on it. But that means we may be building a virtual cell that's really a virtual transcriptome. It can look very predictive within its own modality and still miss the phenotypes that actually matter for disease.

And a subtler point is that a lot of our historical data is observational rather than interventional. You can have huge atlases of cells, which are incredibly useful, but correlation across cell states isn't the same as knowing what happens when you push on the system. If you want models that can actually reason causally (if I knock down this gene, or activate this pathway, what happens?), you need perturbation data, ideally at scale, across many contexts, combinatorially. That's a big reason we've invested so heavily in generating large-scale perturbation atlases rather than just relying on what's in public repositories.

There's also the bias toward what's already been studied. The literature is heavily concentrated on a few thousand well-characterized genes. If you train on that, your model will be confident about the famous genes and weak exactly where discovery is most valuable, in the dark matter of the genome.

So the way I think about it is that data generation has to be designed for the model, not just repurposed for it. You want to be deliberate about diversity of cell contexts, about measuring multiple modalities, about systematic rather than hypothesis-driven sampling, and about having a tight lab-in-the-loop cycle where the model tells you where it's uncertain and you go run those experiments. That closed loop is, I think, where biology is going to start looking more like an engineering discipline. But if we're careless about the data, we'll just build very sophisticated models of our own experimental artifacts.

r001.rationale: The response discusses generalization across cell types and tissues, but does not state that a perfect mouse biology model may fail to model human biology.

r002.rationale: It advocates broader context, modality, and perturbation data, but does not call for substantially more experiments in humans.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think this is actually one of the most underappreciated problems in the field. Everyone talks about model architecture, scaling laws, how many parameters. But in biology, the model is only ever as good as the measurements it was trained on, and the way we generate those measurements is deeply shaped by what humans decided to look at.

Think about how most biological data gets produced. A grad student has a hypothesis. They design an experiment to test it. They pick a cell line, a readout, a set of perturbations. And the dataset that comes out reflects all those choices. It's not a random sample of biology. It's a sample of the questions people thought were interesting, in the systems that were convenient to work in. So when you aggregate decades of that into a training set, you inherit an enormous amount of bias. HEK293 cells and HeLa cells are massively overrepresented. Certain protein families get studied because they're druggable or because the assays exist. Huge swaths of the genome are basically dark.

The second issue is that experimental data in biology is noisy in ways that are hard to disentangle from signal. Batch effects, differences in reagents, differences in how a particular lab handles their cells. If you train a model across many datasets, it will happily learn to predict which lab generated the data, because that's often a stronger signal than the underlying biology. So you have to be really careful about what you're actually learning.

And then there's the question of what you're measuring at all. A lot of what we call functional genomics is really a proxy. Cell viability, fluorescence from a reporter, a transcript count. These are a few dimensions projected out of a very high dimensional system. A model trained on viability screens learns about viability. It doesn't automatically learn about the thing you actually care about, which might be some subtle change in cell state or a disease phenotype that only shows up in a tissue context.

So the way I think about it is that in language or vision, the data was essentially already out there, generated by billions of people doing their thing, and the task was to collect it. In biology we don't have that luxury. We have to decide what to measure, and those decisions are the real bottleneck. That's why I'm pretty convinced the next big leaps won't come from just throwing bigger models at existing public data. They'll come from designing experiments specifically to produce the kind of dense, systematic, unbiased data that models need. Perturbation at scale, many cell types, many contexts, measurements chosen for information content rather than for testing one hypothesis. Essentially letting the model tell you what to measure next. If you don't close that loop, you end up with a very sophisticated model of our historical scientific attention rather than a model of biology.

r001.rationale: The response discusses overrepresented cell lines and context-dependent measurements, but does not state that a perfect mouse biology model may fail to model human biology.

r002.rationale: It advocates designing more systematic experiments across cell types and contexts, but does not specifically call for substantially more experiments in humans.

astra-6.text:
I think the choice of what you measure really defines what your model has a chance to learn. In biology, we often collect data because an assay is scalable or convenient, and then implicitly treat that measurement as a description of the whole system. But gene expression, for example, is only one window into what a cell is doing. It doesn’t capture every aspect of protein activity, spatial organization, or how that cell responds over time.

There’s also the question of which biological contexts you sample. If your training data comes from a narrow set of cell types under fairly artificial conditions, a model might perform very well on held-out examples from that same experiment and still fail when you move to a different tissue or disease state.

So the experimental design is part of the modeling problem. You need to ask: What do I want to predict, and what experiments would actually distinguish the possible explanations? Perturbations can be especially useful there, because observing two things change together isn’t the same as knowing what happens when you intervene. More data helps, but it matters enormously which data you choose to generate.

r001.rationale: The response discusses models failing across tissues or disease states, but does not state that even a perfect mouse biology model may fail to model human biology.

r002.rationale: It says more data and useful experiments matter, but does not advocate conducting substantially more experiments in humans.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the data you choose to collect puts a ceiling on what your model can learn. In biology, we often measure what’s convenient: a handful of cell lines, a particular assay, one time point. And then we want the model to tell us what happens in a patient, across different tissues, over time. That’s a pretty big gap.

Take a genetic perturbation. Its effect can depend on the cell type, the environment, and what other genes are doing. If your experiments don’t vary those contexts, the model has no way to learn how much they matter. It can look very accurate on held-out data from the same experimental setup and still fail when you move into a different biological setting.

So I think experimental design and model development have to be coupled. The question isn’t just, ‘How do we collect more data?’ It’s, ‘Which experiment would distinguish between our competing explanations, or expose where the model is wrong?’ That’s how you start building models that can predict something beyond the experiments you’ve already done.

r001.rationale: The response says models trained in one experimental setup may fail in a different biological setting, but it does not state that a perfect model of mouse biology may fail to model human biology.

r002.rationale: The response advocates choosing experiments that test competing explanations or expose model errors, but it does not advocate conducting substantially more experiments in humans.
